Marissa / Laura,

Thanks again for the demo last week — seeing the dedicated latency profile made the difference for our product team. Attached are our proposed redlines to Exhibit A of the Order Form. The primary ask from legal and product is straightforward: we need explicit downstream productization rights (including sublicensing to our customers) and an absolute prohibition on using our customer data or generated outputs to train or improve Redwood models.

Key asks in the draft:
- Customer to retain exclusive title to all Outputs generated by Customer prompts (including derivatives).
- No use of Customer Outputs, prompts, or telemetry for model training, tuning, or improving services without explicit, opt-in written consent.
- If Redwood requests telemetry for product improvements, that must be anonymized, aggregated, and require a narrow feedback license — not ownership.

We appreciate the standard commercial need for telemetry, but the product team will not accept a broad feedback license that grants training rights. Procurement is on a tight cycle — target signature by 2026-05-20. Can you confirm who on Redwood legal will own the response and whether Redwood can provide a counter that includes a priced opt-out for training?

Attached: Orbit_OrderForm_Redlines_v1.docx (redlines + rationale)

Best,

Susan —

Thanks for sending this over and for the clarity on Orbit's product needs. We want to be accommodating and keep the procurement timeline. High level from Redwood: we can grant broad downstream use rights for Outputs (so your customers can productize), but we need a limited feedback license to operate and improve the service (latency fixes, ops signals, anomaly detection). That license is narrow, system-level, and anonymized — it does not give Redwood ownership of customer Outputs.

Proposed path forward (attached counter):
- Redwood will grant Customer a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive right to use and sublicense Outputs for productization.
- Redwood will agree not to use Customer Outputs or prompt content for training or model improvement unless Customer opts in via a separate written agreement (training opt-in).
- Redwood requests a telemetry/feedback license limited to: aggregated usage metrics, error rates, perf traces, and a tokenization-level telemetry stream that is pseudonymized and filtered for PII. This license is only for service quality/improvement and not for model training.
- Pricing: we can include a priced opt-out (Customer pays uplift to block all operational telemetry) or a priced opt-in for training (revenue share / credit). We propose a single-line pricing appendix in the Order Form.

I've attached a counter Exhibit A (redwood_exhibitA_counter_v2.docx) with concrete language and three options (default telemetry, opt-out with uplift, opt-in training compensation). Can Laura or Ben pick the preferred option and we can route to legal for sign-off.

Action items:
- Laura: review redlines and confirm which of our three options you want to push as baseline.
- Susan: can Orbit confirm whether sublicense to end customers is mandatory or preferred? We used "may sublicense" language to be safe.
- Procurement: target signature date acknowledged (2026-05-20).

Marissa / Ben —

Quick internal note after reading Orbit's redlines and Marissa's counter: legal should avoid an all-or-nothing stance on training prohibition. Our standard approach (and what reduces churn for us) is:

1) Default: No training from Customer Outputs (we honor opt-out by default in the contract language you sent).
2) Option A (Customer opt-in): Customer can explicitly opt in to allow training on a dataset subset under negotiated terms (compensation/credits + data handling SLA).
3) Option B (Customer opt-out via uplift): Customer can pay a telemetry privacy uplift to completely block operational telemetry; this requires a pricing appendix and will increase unit costs.

Operational concerns: if we don't retain a narrow, anonymized telemetry feed we will lose SLO troubleshooting capability and will need to raise pricing or reserve runbook costs. Let's capture that in the pricing appendix and in the Exhibit as an explicit tradeoff.

Suggested edits are inline in Marissa's counter. I also recommend we prepare a short one‑page "privacy & telemetry safeguards" PDF (to attach) that explains what fields we collect, how we pseudonymize, and retention windows. That often gets Orbit procurement comfortable.

I can push this by EOD and flag the pricing uplift options.

—Laura
